headline: Great Point Rip, First Light: Albies Punching Bait, Bonito Stacked Behind Them
subhead: The warm-water edge we've been watching all September finally shoved into the Sound, and the rip off Great Point turned into a washing machine of albies, bonito, and bluefish.
body_markdown:
Stood on the bluff above Great Point Tuesday morning and watched a tern wall drop out of nowhere over the rip line — thirty birds folding into the water in one spot, then the whole thing sliding fifty yards east on the current in about four minutes. That's albies working bait against the rip, and when the terns move that fast and that tight, there's fish under every dive. By the time the sun cleared the horizon there was a second, smaller commotion working the inside edge — shorter, choppier splashes, less white water. That's the bonito signature, and it's been showing up alongside the albies all week from Great Point down through the Nantucket Shoals edge.

We flagged this a few days back — said the albie and bonito push building on the fringes of the warm water would keep extending and add a real secondary target behind the fluke bite. That's exactly what's playing out. The warm filament that's been parked off Rhode Island all September finally leaned north and east, and it's dragging both species with it. Surface temps in the Sound are holding in the high 60s to low 70s depending on where you check — warm enough that bait is staying up and tight rather than diving, which is why the blitzes have been visible and sustained instead of the usual pop-up-and-vanish albie chaos.

Wind's been the swing factor. A stretch of light southwest breeze mid-week kept the rips clean and glassy in the early hours, which is when the Great Point and Sankaty blitzes have been most reliable — first two hours of light, before any boat traffic or thermal breeze stirs things up. When the wind clocked more westerly and picked up Thursday, the bite pushed later into the morning as the bait held deeper against the chop. Watch that pattern into the weekend — if the breeze stays under 10 knots out of the south or southwest, dawn is still the play. If it swings hard west or northwest, give it until mid-morning for the tide and light to line back up.

Tactics have been simple and unforgiving — these fish want speed and small profiles. Half-ounce to three-quarter-ounce epoxy jigs in bone or pearl, worked on a fast, erratic retrieve, have been the most consistent producer on the albies working the Great Point rip on the last two hours of the ebb, when the current stacks bait against the point and the fish pin it there. Deceiver-style flies on intermediate line have worked for the fly crowd willing to strip fast and mend little. The bonito have shown a slight preference for smaller Kastmasters and Deadly Dick-style tins in the quarter-to-half-ounce range — something with a little flash and not much resistance, since bonito are notoriously fussy about anything that doesn't look exactly like the sand eels and silversides they're keyed on right now.

Monomoy has been the other story worth knowing about. With the southwest wind holding for most of the week, the rips off the south end — Monomoy Point and the bars running out toward the Powder Hole — have been setting up clean on the last of the ebb into the start of the flood, and there's been a real striper presence mixing in under the blitzes. Not the size or numbers of a full fall push yet, but enough teens-to-mid-20-inch bass working the same current seams as the albies to make it worth dropping a bucktail or a swimming plug through the wash once the surface action settles. Bluefish have been in the mix too, mostly in the 2-to-4-pound range, chopping up epoxies fast enough that wire or heavy fluoro leader is worth the trouble if you're tired of losing jigs.

Fluke haven't disappeared, they've just taken a back seat to the visual chaos topside. Horseshoe Shoal and the deeper edges around the west end of the Sound are still giving up keeper fluke on the drift — bucktail and Gulp combinations in white or chartreuse, fished slow along the bottom in 20 to 35 feet, still connecting for boats willing to put in bottom time between blitz sightings. It's not the headline story right now, but it's a solid fallback on a morning when the birds haven't shown yet.

Looking at the next few days, the pattern has real legs. The warm edge that pushed this bait and these fish north isn't showing signs of retreating, and with the moon building toward more tidal push over the coming week, expect the rip current at Great Point and off Sankaty to sharpen up and concentrate bait even more. That should mean tighter, more predictable blitz windows rather than the fish being scattered across open water. If the wind stays manageable out of the south or southwest, the smart move is first light at Great Point on the tail of the ebb, working out toward Monomoy as the sun climbs if the bite there goes quiet. Keep a rod rigged light for albies and bonito and a second rigged heavier for whatever bass and blues show up underneath — this time of year in the Sound, you genuinely don't know which one's going to show first until the birds tell you.
